idiom_name: struct node + path slice of frames, sibling slices cloned (slices.Clone)
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types and no persistent collections, so the tree is a struct with a kind field and a children slice, the location is a struct holding the focused node value plus a slice of frames, and each frame carries the parent value and the sibling slices split around the hole. Moves append to and pop that slice, and the rebuild of a parent is an append of cloned sibling slices - slices.Clone (Go 1.21+) is the primitive that keeps the old version valid, because Go slices alias their backing array and an in-place append would mutate both trees. Immutability is therefore a copying discipline enforced by hand, not by the language; the clojure.zip-style package github.com/mikowitz/gander has exactly this shape and documents its cost - the ancestor path is copied on each Down step, giving O(N^2) allocation for a traversal to depth N.
pitfalls: Slices alias their backing array: appending to or writing into a shared child slice mutates the previous tree too, so any rebuild must start from slices.Clone (Go 1.21+) of the siblings.
There are no sum types, so the closed node set is a kind field plus a union of fields or `any`; a forgotten case is a runtime panic instead of a compile error.
A frame storing the parent node copies it, including its child-slice header - cheap, but shallow, so the parent's children must never be appended to in place.
Nothing in the language prevents a caller from mutating the focused node, and exporting a frame's sibling slices hands out write access to the tree.
